item.title: Investigation of Cu(II) Binding by Human Calprotectin Reveals an Unusual Fluxional Coordination Environment
item.description:
Abstract
Human calprotectin (CP, S100A8/S100A9 heterooligomer) is a multi-metal sequestering protein that contributes to the innate immune response by starving invading microbial pathogens of essential metal nutrients. Despite the ability of CP to withhold copper from microbial pathogens, its copper coordination chemistry is largely unexplored. Here we elucidate the Cu(II)-binding properties of CP-Ser [S100A8(C42S)/S100A9(C3S) variant] under conditions of high and low Ca(II) and present a working model for how CP sequesters Cu(II). Our biochemical and spectroscopic studies reveal that both the His3Asp and His6 sites bind Cu(II) with Ca(II)-dependent affinity, and Cu(II) binding to both sites is required for Cu(II)-dependent self-association of CP heterodimers to heterotetramers. Moreover, our spectroscopic data demonstrate that Cu(II) binds to the His6 site in a fluxional coordination environment, and that the mode of Cu(II) binding is allosterically modulated by Ca(II) coordination to the EF-hand domains and Cu(II) binding at the His3Asp site. Sequestration of Cu(II) using a fluxional His6 site contrasts with how CP captures other nutrient M(II) (M = Mn, Fe, Ni, Zn) at this site using a static and nearly idealized octahedral binding mode. This study reveals the remarkable ability of a fluxional site to participate in metal sequestration at the host–pathogen interface.

item.title: Nucleotide-Resolved Conformational Analysis of Nascent RNA Chains within the Bacterial Transcription Elongation Complex by MAS-DNP Solid-State NMR
item.description:
Abstract
In all kingdoms of life, multisubunit RNA polymerases transcribe DNA to RNA. Both genomic DNA and newly transcribed RNA play key roles in transcription initiation, elongation, and termination. For example, a stretch of uridine residues at the 3′-end of the nascent RNA chain serves as a trigger to terminate transcription, release the nascent RNA chain, and disassemble bacterial transcription elongation complexes (ECs). It has remained unclear how the transcript can trigger termination if polyuridine stretches are synthesized. Here, we establish an approach that combines site-selective 13C/15N labeling of uridines with magic-angle-spinning dynamic nuclear polarization (MAS-DNP) NMR to probe the nascent transcript residue by residue within a reconstituted, stalled Escherichia coli transcription EC. We read out the 3′-terminal U-tract in the free RNA and in complexes stalled at two registers to investigate conformational heterogeneity in the rU–dA hybrid duplex. Our results suggest that the internal uridines adopt a stable A-form (C3′-endo) conformation in the hybrid duplex. This conformation remains unchanged within the EC, whereas the 3′-terminal residue is selectively perturbed within the complex. Solid-state NMR data collected on tailored isotopically labeled ECs resolve single-residue differences in conformation inside an assembled transcription EC, opening a route to study the nascent RNA at sites relevant to pausing and termination by MAS-DNP.

item.title: Antibody-Guided Photocatalytic Cross-Linking Enables Targeted Protein Structure Elucidation
item.description:
Abstract
The structure and dynamics of proteins underlie virtually all biological processes, and there is a growing need for methods that can interrogate protein conformations in complex mixtures. Chemical cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) addresses this need. Still, it relies on untargeted, diffusible cross-linkers that react with any accessible residue, limiting both selectivity and effective use of cross-linking capacity. Here, we report an antibody-guided, photocatalytic cross-linking platform that enables targeted structural elucidation of proteins of interest within complex samples. We developed HyProX, a trifunctional histidine-specific cross-linker that combines two hydrazide groups to trap light-induced histidine intermediates and a phosphonic acid handle for enrichment. Building on LUX-MS photocatalytic proximity labeling, singlet oxygen generators (SOGs) conjugated to antibodies locally convert histidines on the target protein into short-lived endoperoxide intermediates, which HyProX selectively captures to form His–His cross-links in a strictly light-dependent manner. Using model peptides, we demonstrate efficient formation of cross-linked products and show that HyProX forms a C–N bond that undergoes preferential collision-induced dissociation (CID), releasing signature fragment pairs that MS3 can directly sequence. Applying antibody-guided HyProX cross-linking to human transferrin in a multiprotein mixture and human serum yields an increase in cross-linked spectral matches and higher unique cross-link coverage for the target protein compared to untargeted conditions, with all observed cross-links mapping on the known crystal structure. Together, these results establish antibody-guided, photocatalytic His–His cross-linking with HyProX as a conceptually new XL-MS platform that provides spatiotemporal control, residue selectivity, and an intrinsic MS-based decross-linking readout for targeted protein structure analysis in complex biological mixtures.

item.title: Rh 2 C 3 − Cluster-Driven Nitrogen Activation: Trapping a High-Energy Intermediate
item.description:
Abstract
Converting inert and globally abundant molecules such as N2 into useful chemicals is central to sustainable energy and environmental chemistry. Herein, we investigate the gas-phase reaction of the Rh2C3− anion with N2 using mass spectrometry, anion photoelectron spectroscopy, and quantum chemical calculations. The experimental spectra of Rh2C3− and Rh2C3N2− exhibit closely similar features, indicating a preserved electronic core upon N2 attachment. Theoretical analysis further reveals that the end-on N2 adsorption complex is a trapped high-energy intermediate whose subsequent transformation is prevented by an activation barrier that necessitates additional energy input, and that this complex exhibits superior performance in the coconversion of diverse energy-bearing gas molecules. Furthermore, the subsequent application of oriented external electric fields provides a nondestructive and continuously adjustable means of modifying the intrinsic barrier heights, thereby effectively switching the reaction mechanism. These findings elucidate the complex reaction network of Rh2C3− with N2, establish a reliable spectroscopic fingerprint for identifying isomeric intermediates, and provide fundamental insights into electronic control strategies for catalytic nitrogen activation.

item.title: Departing Pathways in Aza-Diarylethene Photoswitching: Elucidating the Role of the Central Ring Allows Reprogramming of the Photoresponse
item.description:
Abstract
Aza-diarylethenes (aza-DAEs) are an emerging class of molecular photoswitches that allow reversible C–N bond formation and cleavage upon irradiation. They not only show high potential as T-type photochromes but also offer exciting opportunities for the exploration of unique reactivity control. Two types of these photoswitches are currently being investigated, which differ substantially in the nature of their metastable states. While classical DAE behavior is found in perfluorinated thiazole derivatives, an unexpected zwitterion formation and concomitant aromatization is observed for nonfluorinated pyrimidine derivatives. The latter offers reversible control over intramolecular charge separation and intrinsic three-state photoswitching. Their metastable state unleashes thiolate reactivity, which can be harnessed, e.g., in photoinitiation applications for smart polymer generation. Despite this promising progress, the reason for the divergent photochemical behavior in aza-DAEs is not yet understood. Here, we show that substitution of the central five-membered ring is responsible for the different photochemical outcomes and nature of the metastable state. Furthermore, our computational results provide systematic insights into the structural factors governing the relative stability of the neutral closed-ring and zwitterionic forms. We then use this knowledge to reprogram thioazole derivatives and render them into zwitterion-forming aza-DAEs. With these results, the predictable and rational design of aza-DAEs is enabled, which can now be radically changed in their photoresponses and tailored to specific desired properties and applications.

item.title: Stepwise Assembly of a Lavandulyl Moiety on Flavonoids Enabled by a 2″-Prenyltransferase
item.description:
Abstract
Lavandulylated flavonoids contain a characteristic branched C10 moiety, and the enzymatic basis underlying its biosynthesis remains poorly understood. Here, we elucidate the complete biosynthetic pathway of the lavandulylated flavonoid kurarinone from naringenin in the medicinal plant Sophora flavescens. The pathway involves four sequential steps, 8-prenylation, 2′-hydroxylation, 2″-prenylation, and 5-O-methylation, catalyzed by Sf8PT, SfF2′H, Sf2″PT, and Sf5OMT, respectively. Sf2′′PT represents the first characterized flavonoid 2′′-prenyltransferase (PT), catalyzing a second prenylation on the pre-existing prenyl side chain to complete the assembly of the branched lavandulyl moiety. The activity of Sf2″PT strictly depends on prior 2′-hydroxylation, establishing a defined order of enzymatic modifications that enables this noncanonical prenylation reaction. Ancestral sequence reconstruction and mutagenesis demonstrated that an inactive ancestral enzyme could be converted into functional 8PT or 2′′PT variants through one or seven amino acid substitutions, respectively. Collectively, this work establishes the enzymatic basis for stepwise lavandulyl moiety assembly and provides a framework for the enzymatic construction and engineering of branched prenylated natural products.

item.title: Hydrogen-Bond Network-Assisted Ethylene and Hydrogen Photosynthesis from Methane over Isolated Ir Active Sites under Ambient Conditions
item.description:
Abstract
Direct conversion of methane to ethylene (DCM) is an attractive yet formidable challenge due to the difficult C–H activation and uncontrollable C–C coupling process. Herein, we report a hydrogen-bond network-assisted ethylene and H2 photosynthesis from methane over oxygen-vacancy-enriched TiO2-supported single Ir atoms (Ir1/TiO2–Ov) under ambient conditions. The Ir-induced lattice distortion drives spontaneous hydrolysis under humid conditions, generating a hydroxylated surface that endows coordinatively unsaturated Ir sites to activate the first methane molecule without light irradiation. Upon photoexcitation, surface hydroxyls are oxidized into dangling oxygen species (*O) on Ti sites, which promote the dehydrogenation of *CH3 to *CH2. In synergy with the Ir site, the adjacent *O species activate a second CH4 molecule and finally direct selective C–C coupling to form C2H4. Meanwhile, methane-derived protons migrate through the hydrogen-bond network via a Grotthuss mechanism to produce H2. The Ir1/TiO2–Ov catalyst achieves the production of ethylene (14.3 ± 0.7 μmol•gcat–1•h–1) and H2 (28.4 ± 1.2 μmol•gcat–1•h–1) for at least 210 h at 25 °C and atmospheric pressure under light irradiation. Our findings establish a hydrogen-bond network-assisted strategy for methane C–H activation and selective C–C and H–H coupling.

item.title: Redox-Window-Guided Metal Node Editing of Copper Metal–Organic Frameworks for Recyclable Heterogeneous Cu(I) Catalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Cu(I) catalysts are central to many bond-forming reactions, but integrating Cu(I) sites into recyclable porous solids remains difficult because Cu(I) is easily oxidized, over-reduced, or leached. Here, we report redox-window-guided metal node editing as an oxidation-state-programming strategy that converts hydrolytically fragile Cu(II)3BTC2 into a hydrolytically stable mixed-valence Cu(I/II) MOF catalyst. Phenolic reductants are selected by matching their oxidation potentials to the Cu(II)–to–Cu(I) window of Cu(II)3BTC2, enabling proton-coupled, inner-sphere single-electron transfer at Cu paddlewheel nodes. Hydroquinone gives the most controlled material, [p-Ph(OH)2]-Cu3BTC2, containing 33.4% Cu(I), ship-in-a-bottle [Cu(MeCN)4]+ complexes, mesopores, and enhanced stability under humid, acidic, and basic conditions. As a heterogeneous catalyst for hydrative amide synthesis, [p-Ph(OH)2]-Cu3BTC2 affords 92% yield, negligible Cu leaching, five-cycle recyclability, and the highest turnover number among compared Cu(I) catalysts.

item.title: Synthetic Control of Quantum Phases in Organic Conductors: Molecular-Level Disorder Engineering and Pressure-Induced Superconductivity
item.description:
Abstract
Structural randomness is a dominant factor governing electronic properties; however, the intrinsic effects of a disordered potential remain elusive due to the lack of a synthetic platform capable of introducing purely random potentials without carrier doping or altering the fundamental band structure. Here, we demonstrate the synthetic control of superconducting and insulating phases by exploiting the unique conformational flexibility of molecular conductors. Through precise thermodynamic control during crystal growth, we selectively synthesize the structurally ordered superconductor κ-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu[N(CN)2]Br (κ-Br; BEDT-TTF = bis(ethylenedithio)tetrathiafulvalene) and the structurally disordered insulating polymorph, κ″-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu[N(CN)2]Br (κ″-Br), possessing the exact same chemical composition. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations confirm the metastable nature of κ″-Br, showing a packing arrangement of BEDT-TTF molecules and an electronic band structure nearly identical to those of superconducting κ-Br, but featuring a disordered anion layer. Optical conductivity spectra reveal low-energy excitations without a distinct gap, indicating that the insulating behavior originates from disorder-induced carrier localization. Furthermore, κ″-Br undergoes a pressure-induced insulator–superconductor transition, in stark contrast to postsynthetic X-ray irradiation which induced irreversible structural damage. This work represents the first demonstration of synthetic control of an ordered superconductor and a disordered insulator driven solely by orientational disorder in organic conductors. Our study provides new avenues for manipulating strongly correlated electron systems and for investigating the intrinsic effects of randomness, free from carrier doping or structural perturbation of conducting layers.

item.title: Single-Atom Cerium Unlocks Efficient Hydrogen Spillover within Nonreducible Zeolites through a Proton–Electron Relay
item.description:
Abstract
Hydrogen spillover connects hydrogen activation with spatially separated catalytic functions, yet engineering efficient hydrogen transport through nonreducible zeolites remains an outstanding challenge owing to the absence of intrinsic pathways for coupled proton–electron transfer. Here, we show that isolated cerium atoms incorporated into Pt/USY transform the zeolite from a passive support into an active medium for solid-state hydrogen transport. In situ spectroscopy, isotopic tracing, and theoretical calculations reveal that atomically dispersed Ce species dynamically generate localized hydroxyl groups and oxygen vacancies that cooperatively establish a proton–electron relay, substantially lowering the kinetic barrier for hydrogen migration through zeolitic micropores. The resulting enhancement in hydrogen spillover extends hydrogen delivery to spatially remote Brønsted acid sites, suppresses coke formation, and significantly improves polyolefin hydrocracking stability. These findings establish hydrogen transport as a tunable design parameter in bifunctional zeolite catalysis and provide a general strategy for engineering hydrogen-transfer pathways in nonreducible porous materials.

item.title: Electron-Deficient β-Diketone Ligand Enabled Ni-Catalyzed Remote Dicarbofunctionalization of Alkenes
item.description:
Abstract
A nickel-catalyzed remote migratory dicarbofunctionalization of alkenes was realized with high efficiency and excellent regioselectivity without the assistance of a directing group. The formation of a thermodynamically stable allyl-metal intermediate and the use of an electron-deficient β-diketone ligand are the keys to the success of these remote diarylation and arylalkenylation. This protocol features a broad substrate scope and excellent functional group compatibility, providing a series of remote diarylated and arylalkenylated hydrocarbons in high yields. Notably, the allyl group represents one of the most synthetically useful handles in synthetic chemistry, and the synthetic values of this process have been demonstrated by the formal synthesis of allocolchicinoids, and by the preparation of a RARγ selective retinoid agonist in a highly efficient and step-economical manner.

item.title: Strengthening Metal–Oxygen Bonds via Ionicity–Covalency Asymmetric Connection: 4f Electronic Configuration Effect
item.description:
Abstract
Precise control over the characteristics of metal–oxygen (M–O) bonds by regulating the electron redistribution between the metal and oxygen under perturbation conditions is crucial for maintaining the structural stability of transition-metal oxides. However, its development has always been hindered by the strong coupling between orbital hybridization and charge localization. Herein, by leveraging the strong ionicity of the Ce–O bonds in CeO2, we constructed an ionicity–covalency asymmetric bonding network, in which the ionic Ce–O is atomically coupled with the covalent M–O (M = Ni/Co). The reduced Ce–O coordination in this special structure weakens the O 2p → Ce 4f charge transfer and further elevates the ionic character of Ce–O bonds, thereby activating the reversible 4f electronic configuration transition. Critically, this configuration undergoes reversible transformation under potential fluctuation, reshaping charge redistribution within the M–O bonding motifs and then suppressing irreversible M–O bond degradation. Harnessing this mechanism enables transition-metal oxides to express a robust framework for the whole structure under repeated redox cycling. Incorporating this resulting CeO2/NiCo2O4, a large-scale alkaline water electrolysis (AWE) stack delivers significantly stable operation for over 350 h at 6 A under a 12-h intermittent experimental protocol. This finding offers a fundamental insight into the dynamic charge distribution in M–O bonds under potential perturbation for universal structural protection.

item.title: Revisiting the Biosynthetic Cyclization of Indole Sesquiterpene Alkaloids: Proposal of a Spiro -Indolenine Pathway and Synthesis of Prelecanindole
item.description:
Abstract
Indole sesquiterpene and indole diterpene alkaloids constitute a distinctive class of natural products characterized by complex polycyclic ring architectures and diverse potent biological activities. In indole sesquiterpenes, the characteristic indole-containing pentacyclic skeleton is biosynthesized from 3-farnesylindole through epoxidation followed by a sequential cationic cyclization. Although the cyclization enzyme has been identified, the details of its cyclization mechanism remain unclear. Here, we propose a new biosynthetic mechanism involving a spiro-indoleninium intermediate, which contrasts with the long-standing mechanism proposed in the 1970s that proceeds via a tertiary-to-secondary carbocation rearrangement. We demonstrated the feasibility of this new mechanism by means of density functional theory (DFT) calculations, which do not support the conventional mechanism and also by chemical emulation: the putative spiro-indolenine intermediate was synthesized from two fragments through stereoselective cyclopropanation as a key reaction and subsequently converted to prelecanindole, a common biosynthetic intermediate of indole sesquiterpene alkaloids, under mild acidic conditions.

item.title: A Bioinspired Thiolate-Bridged Diiron System for Functionally Replicating Hydrazine Dehydrogenase and Its Efficient Electrocatalytic Hydrazine Oxidation
item.description:
Abstract
Hydrazine dehydrogenase (HDH) catalyzes the oxidation of hydrazine (N2H4) to dinitrogen (N2) as the final step of anaerobic ammonium oxidation, an essential process in closing the nitrogen cycle. Despite extensive biochemical studies, the detailed mechanism of HDH at a molecular level remains elusive. An increasing number of studies indicate that the hydrazine oxidation reaction (HzOR) is also central to direct hydrazine fuel cells. However, known electrocatalysts for HzOR are predominantly heterogeneous systems, while molecular electrocatalysts are still scarce, especially those inspired by biological HDH. This scarcity not only limits mechanistic understanding but also hinders the development of efficient and tunable catalysts. To tackle these challenging issues, we sought inspiration from the biological HDH system, wherein multiple iron-containing heme subunits cooperatively promote efficient HzOR with the assistance of surrounding sulfur-bearing cysteine residues. Integrating these key features, we selected the thiolate-bridged diiron complex [Cp*Fe(μ-SEt)(MeCN)]2[PF6]2 (1, Cp* = η5-C5Me5) for functionally replicating HDH. Treatment of 1 with N2H4 induces disproportionation to afford the active diazene (N2H2) species, which can be captured by the diiron cooperative platform to yield [Cp*Fe(μ-SEt)2(cis-μ-η1:η1-HN=NH)FeCp*][PF6] (2). In the presence of appropriate electron and proton acceptors, complex 2 undergoes a two-electron oxidation, leading to N2 release and the regeneration of 1. Remarkably, both complexes 1 and 2 serve as efficient molecular electrocatalysts for HzOR. This diiron molecular system not only achieves the functional replication of HDH involving a key N2H2 intermediate but also establishes a bioinspired design strategy for developing multimetal cooperative electrocatalysts toward efficient HzOR.

item.title: Electrochemical Allylic Carboxylation of Unactivated Alkenes with CO 2
item.description:
Abstract
As both alkenes and CO2 are abundant and easily available feedstocks, carboxylation of alkenes with CO2 represents an attractive and sustainable strategy to synthesize value-added carboxylic acids. Despite substantial advances in carboxylation of π-bonds in alkenes, the carboxylation of C–H bonds in alkenes, which preserves the C═C bond in the synthesis of valuable unsaturated carboxylic acids, remains a longstanding challenge, particularly for unactivated alkenes owing to their intrinsically low reactivity. Herein, we report the first electrochemical allylic carboxylation of unactivated alkenes with CO2, providing a direct and selective approach to hard-to-obtain β,γ-unsaturated carboxylic acids. Moreover, this reaction exhibits a broad substrate scope, good functional group tolerance, and applicability to late-stage diversification. Mechanistic studies indicate that the electrogenerated CO2 radical anion acts both as the carboxylation reagent and the hydrogen-atom abstraction species for the subsequent desaturation process, further uncovering the synthetic utility potential of the CO2 radical anion.

item.title: Immobilizing Ionomers by Strong Hydrogen Bonds for Highly Stable Industrial Water Electrolysis at 3.0 A/cm 2
item.description:
Abstract
Raising the operating current density can effectively reduce the high cost of proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs), but this approach is limited by rapid electrode degradation. Our previous research identified a critical degradation mechanism in which ionomer migration blocks mass-transport channels in the anode catalyst layer (ACL). Here, we find that each sulfonate group of the ionomer forms only about half a hydrogen bond on the IrO2 surface, indicating a weak catalyst–ionomer interaction. Rather than modifying the IrO2 surface, we propose to introduce additives that provide additional adsorption sites forming stronger hydrogen bonds (SHB) with the sulfonate groups. The resulting SHB-ACL maintains a stable ionomer distribution and pore network even after aging, and exhibits a roughly four fold lower degradation rate over 2500 h at 3.0 A/cm2. Furthermore, the electrode can be readily scaled up to 600 cm2. The improvement stability is at least in part attributable to enhanced interface interaction, although preserved porosity, water/gas transport, and interparticle contacts may also contribute. These findings offer a scalable route toward durable industrial PEMWE devices.

item.title: Ligand-Controlled Chemodivergent β-Methylene C(sp 3 )–H Heteroarylation of Aliphatic Acids
item.description:
Abstract
Achieving ligand-controlled chemodivergence in C–H activation is still difficult because several competing reaction pathways are available when multiple C–H bonds are present. We describe a Pd(II)-catalyzed, chemodivergent β-methylene C(sp3)–H heteroarylation of free aliphatic acids in which two distinct classes of bidentate pyridone ligands each deliver a different product. These two ligands also overcome a long-standing inhibitory effect of heteroaryl iodides, demonstrating the potential of this protocol to serve as a general C(sp3)–C(sp2) coupling method using readily available aliphatic acids as the alkylating partner. Mechanistic experiments and DFT analyses reveal that π–π stacking between the quinoline motif and the heteroaryl ring lowers the barrier for rotation of the carbon–palladium bond, favoring protodepalladation to the reductive Heck product, whereas the oxime ether ligand lacks this interaction and steers the key intermediate toward β-H elimination to give the oxidative Heck product.

item.title: Cation Pinning toward High-Concentration Formic Acid Fuel Cells
item.description:
Abstract
Despite the high theoretical energy density of concentrated formic acid, direct formic acid fuel cells (DFAFCs) incorporating conventional nanoparticle or emerging single-atom anodes exhibit a precipitous power loss as fuel concentration scales. While CO poisoning is traditionally blamed, we show that this limitation is governed by interfacial acid–base kinetics. By implementing a cation-pinning strategy via rare-earth oxide-modified Rh single-atom sites, we stabilize OH– from water dissociation through interfacial ionic anchoring to trigger localized pH inversion. This modulation leads to the preferential enrichment of interfacial formate, identified here as the primary reactive species. Consequently, Dy2O3–Rh/NC delivers a mass activity 641-fold higher than that of nanoparticle benchmarks. The resulting anode achieves an exceptional peak power density of 375 mW cm–2, surpassing commercial Pd/C across all concentrations. This work establishes precision ionic management as a versatile approach to breaking performance limits in multiphase catalysis.

item.title: In Situ High-Pressure NMR Reveals Pressure-Defect Generation in Aluminum Acetylacetonate toward Integrated Optical Response
item.description:
Abstract
Stimuli-responsive luminescent materials featuring real-time pressure-response with persistent memory effects hold considerable promise for advanced photonic computing. However, most pressure-memory behavior depends on triggered irreversible phase transitions, which hinders the integration of reversible optical sensing. Synergistic pressure treatment and defect generation serve as an effective approach that ensures the phase-transition-free structure while affording excellent photoluminescence (PL) performance. In this work, we employ pressure-defect generation strategy in aluminum acetylacetonate that effectively integrates short-term pressure response with long-term history memory. Notably, the PL wavelength acts as a digital readout across 476–486 nm, alongside an intensity-based analog signal below 4 GPa. Upon crossing this threshold, the response further embeds memory states dependent on pressure history. In situ high-pressure nuclear magnetic resonance (HP-NMR) measurements reveal, from both static and dynamic perspectives, the progressive deepening of pressure-induced local responses within the molecular framework, from ligand-associated modulation to Al–O coordination perturbation. This establishes a two-regime pressure-defect generation pathway: reversible structural distortion induces electronic-state defects, whereas partially trapped severe distortion may generate radical defects. Our work not only highlights the unique capability of local dynamic probing for the design of pressure-responsive materials, but also broadens the horizons of single-material multifunctional information-processing systems.

item.title: Bioinspired Ångström-Scale Coupling of Reductive Centers in Covalent Organic Frameworks Drives Efficient Photocatalytic Oxygen Reduction
item.description:
Abstract
The photocatalytic oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) is crucial for solar-to-chemical energy conversion but faces challenges from weak oxygen adsorption and slow kinetics. Inspired by the spatially cooperative multimetal centers in natural enzymes, we develop a strategy of Å-scale spatial coupling of reductive centers in covalent organic frameworks (COFs). Ortho-amino-functionalized COFs were constructed with catalytic pockets that position multiple acceptors within subnanometer proximity, creating coupled reductive centers for cooperative O2 adsorption and multielectron relay. The optimal framework, with a model-derived separation of approximately 3.3 Å between reductive centers, achieves a hydrogen peroxide production rate of 4.10 mmol g–1 h–1 in pure water under visible light without sacrificial agents, along with a high apparent quantum yield of 19.2% at 450 nm. Practical viability is confirmed through operation in diverse water sources and continuous-flow systems. Moreover, the enhanced ORR activity accelerates oxidative coupling of benzylamine derivatives, showing over 80% conversion for 12 analogues. Experimental and theoretical analyses indicate that the confined neighboring sites enhance O2 adsorption and activation, stabilize •OOH intermediates, and promote the two-electron reduction pathway. This work establishes convergent multicenter coupling as a foundational design principle, unlocking new avenues for the rational creation of high-performance photocatalysts in sustainable chemistry.

item.title: A Cu-Modified Layered Thiostannate for Selective Pb Capture from Strongly Acidic Media
item.description:
Abstract
Layered metal sulfide ion exchangers are powerful platforms for soft-metal capture, but their application in strongly acidic environments requires framework stability while preserving accessible ion-exchange pathways. Here, we introduce a new series of Cu-modified SnS2-derived layered chalcogenides, AMS-8 (A = Na, K, Rb, Cs), featuring labile interlayer alkali metal ions. NMS-8 (Na1.13Cu1.32Sn3.34S8·xH2O) demonstrates that Cu+ can be incorporated into the SnS2-derived AMS layered motif without disrupting the fundamental architecture. Upon acid exposure, NMS-8 undergoes Na+/H+ exchange and interlayer contraction, showing low Sn leaching in 6 M H2SO4 but substantial Sn dissolution in 6 M HCl after prolonged exposure, despite persistent powder X-ray diffraction reflections of the layered phase. NMS-8 can rapidly capture Pb2+ from water, achieving near-complete removal within 20 s under dilute conditions, a Sips-fitted capacity of 178.2 ± 12.4 mg g–1 (regression standard error), and high selectivity against common competing cations. Structural characterization supports preservation of the lamellar network and a proposed structural model featuring Cu+ displaced off-center within a distorted octahedral framework environment. In an acid mine drainage simulant, NMS-8 selectively removes Pb, Cd, and Cu under acidic multicomponent conditions while retaining its layered structure. Local structural characterization of NMS-8@Pb reveals a spatially heterogeneous Pb distribution within individual crystallites that is not appropriately described by a simple homogeneous interlayer exchange model and is consistent with local structural reorganization during Pb2+ uptake. These results highlight Cu-modified layered thiostannates as promising platforms for rapid, selective soft-metal capture, with substantial resistance to concentrated sulfuric acid and Pb retention dependent on the leaching medium.

item.title: Negative-Charge-Transfer Ligand Holes Enhance Ferromagnetism and Topological Transport in van der Waals Magnets
item.description:
Abstract
Many prototypical 3d van der Waals (vdW) magnets contain heavy ligands with closed p shells, whose strong spin–orbit coupling (SOC) influences the magnetism only indirectly through p–d hybridization. Here we show that negative charge transfer (NCT) creates spin-polarized, SOC-active holes in the ligand p states bordering the vdW gap, coupling magnetic exchange and topological transport within the same states. First-principles calculations identify the synthesized MnSiTe3 as an NCT d5L ferromagnet comprising high-spin Mn2+ and one formal Te 5p ligand hole per f.u. The Te-derived holes strengthen both intralayer and, in particular, interlayer ferromagnetic exchange, favoring ferromagnetic over antiferromagnetic interlayer order by a surprisingly large 84.1 meV/f.u. SOC within the partially occupied Te 5p manifold produces an easy-plane magnetocrystalline anisotropy of 3.6 meV/f.u. The resulting simulated Curie temperature reaches 464 K. The SOC-active Te 5p holes further generate multiple Weyl points, yielding a calculated intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity of 760 Ω–1 cm–1 that remains large over a broad energy window around the Fermi level. All those results stand in sharp contrast to ligand-shell-closed vdW magnets. This NCT ligand-hole picture and the resulting magnetic and transport responses also extend to the synthesized MnGeTe3 and the predicted iodides Cr0.5Mn0.5I3 and MnI3. These results establish NCT as a chemical strategy that makes the vdW interface magnetically and topologically active. Substituting later 3d metals or heavier p ligands into existing vdW magnets drives them toward the NCT regime, providing a design principle for the discovery of new NCT candidates.

item.title: Asymmetric Partial Hydrogenation of Quinazolines: Overcoming Catalyst Poisoning by a Robust yet Active Solo-Coordination-Vacant Ir(III) Pincer Catalyst
item.description:
Abstract
Catalytic asymmetric partial hydrogenation of quinazolines to afford enantioenriched 3,4-dihydroquinazolines, a privileged scaffold in medicinal chemistry, is a long-standing challenge likely due to product-induced catalyst deactivation. Here, we report a robust yet highly reactive solo-coordination-vacant Ir(III) pincer catalyst being capable of overcoming this poisoning challenge. This catalyst enables the asymmetric partial hydrogenation of a broad range of quinazolines, affording 3,4-dihydroquinazolines in high yields (up to 98%) and excellent enantioselectivities (up to 99% ee). In a dedicated catalyst-loading study, the loading could be reduced to 0.001 mol % (10 ppm, TON = 38,000). Mechanistic investigations, including NMR spectroscopic detection of a key Ir–H intermediate and base-dependence studies, support a catalytic cycle proceeding through a well-defined Ir(III)-hydride species and suggest that an alkali-metal-assisted pathway is unlikely to be dominant.

item.title: Local Molecular Motions Encode Time-Resolved Infrared Spectra of Proteins
item.description:
Abstract
Time-resolved infrared spectroscopy probes protein dynamics over time scales spanning more than 10 orders of magnitude, yet the molecular motions underlying the observed kinetic signatures have remained elusive. Here we combine transient infrared spectroscopy with nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations to establish a direct connection between experimental relaxation times and local structural motions. Studying single-domain allosteric proteins, we find that inter-residue contact distances provide the structural representation that most faithfully reproduces the experimental dynamics. Correlation analysis identifies localized networks of coordinated contacts that mediate long-range coupling between secondary-structure elements. The characteristic time scales of these contact networks quantitatively match the experimentally observed relaxation processes, enabling each kinetic step to be assigned to a specific molecular motion. Applied to allosteric signal propagation in PDZ3 and photoinduced perturbation of the binding pocket of PDZ2 or a ligand binding to PDZ2, this framework provides an atomistic picture of hierarchical protein relaxation and establishes a general framework for connecting transient infrared spectroscopy with the molecular mechanisms of protein dynamics.

item.title: A Bowl-Shaped B,N-Tetraquinane Organic Super-Reductant
item.description:
Abstract
Developing a stable molecular reductant with exceptionally strong reducing power remains highly challenging. In this work, we synthesized and characterized a bowl-shaped B–N tetraquinane in a single high-yield step. Cyclic voltammetry reveals a reduction potential of −3.2 V vs Fc/Fc+, a new record among organic reductants. This super-reductant enables [3 + 2] cycloadditions with ketones and imines, dearomatization of phthalazine, cleavage of strong C–Si bonds, direct reduction–borylation of fluorobenzene, deoxygenative coupling of nitrosobenzene, and ring-opening C–C coupling of aromatics into polyenes. Computational studies support its synthetic pathway, ring strain, high reactivity, and remarkably negative reduction potential. These findings demonstrate how three-dimensional topological strain can transform a boron-based dianion into a powerful reagent for reductive reactions and demanding bond activations.

item.title: Dynamic Li + /Na + -Exchanging Interphase Stabilizes High-Voltage Ni-Rich Cathodes for 557 Wh kg –1 Lithium Batteries
item.description:
Abstract
High-voltage operation of Ni-rich layered cathodes LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 (NCM811) accelerates electrolyte decomposition at the surface and destabilizes the bulk lattice with oxygen loss. Conventional strategies for regulating the cathode–electrolyte interphase (CEI) commonly suppress persistent parasitic reactions at Ni-rich cathode surfaces, but increase interfacial polarization and offer limited protection against structural degradation in the bulk. Here, a dynamic interphase is constructed by coating NCM811 with a Na+-based solid-electrolyte Na3Zr2Si2PO12 (NZSP). During cycling, Li+/Na+ exchange transforms the NZSP layer into a fast Li+ conducting interphase LixNa3–xZr2Si2PO12 (L-NZSP), while the Na+ ions are incorporated into the NCM811 lattice. The L-NZSP suppresses parasitic reactions at high charging voltages. Meanwhile, the incorporated Na+ ions provide pillar-like support for the layered framework, stabilizing the oxygen lattice and mitigating chemo-mechanical degradation. Consequently, the modified cathode retains 80% capacity after 511 cycles at 4.7 V and enables a 4 Ah pouch cell to deliver 557 Wh kg–1 with 80.5% retention over 118 cycles. This work demonstrates Li+/Na+-exchanging interphase as an effective strategy to couple interfacial protection with bulk lattice reinforcement for high-voltage Ni-rich cathodes in high-energy lithium batteries.

item.title: Subambient Synthesis of Freestanding Monolayer Cubic ZrO 2 Crystals with High Dielectric Permittivity
item.description:
Abstract
Two-dimensional (2D) polymorphic materials offer access to unconventional crystal structures that trigger exotic properties and functionalities beyond equilibrium phases. However, extending this opportunity to metal oxides remains highly challenging because both thickness reduction and phase transformation involve large energy barriers in such strongly bonded ionic structures. Here we report an atomic-freezing conversion strategy that kinetically stabilizes freestanding 2D metastable oxide crystals under subambient conditions. Single-crystalline cubic ZrO2 of monolayer thickness is produced and stabilized below room temperature, although this phase is typically stable only at temperatures above 2000 °C in bulk. Structural analysis reveals that the layered ZrNCl precursor contains a Zr atomic framework that matches the (111) planes of cubic ZrO2. During conversion, suppressed atomic motion under low temperatures and 2D confinement preserves the nonequilibrium cubic structure. The resulting 2D cubic ZrO2 exhibits a high dielectric permittivity of ∼23.5 and enables MoS2 field-effect transistors with an on/off ratio of ∼108 and a subthreshold slope as low as 63.5 mV dec–1. This approach also applies to cubic HfO2 and tetragonal Bi2O3, providing a general kinetic route to bypass thermodynamic phase constraints and expanding access to metastable oxides in the 2D limit.

item.title: Micelle-Driven MOF Degradation for Enhanced Cargo Release in Micromotors
item.description:
Abstract
Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are widely explored as cargo-delivery platforms, yet efficient release of the encapsulated cargo remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate that anionic surfactant micelles actively destabilize the HKUST-1 MOF framework through Cu2+ extraction, converting a typically undesired degradation process into a mechanism for enhanced cargo release. Complementary mechanistic studies reveal that this process depends on surfactant self-assembly and on the accessibility and coordination environment of the metal nodes. The resulting framework destabilization greatly enhances the release of different cargos from HKUST-1. This mechanistic concept is subsequently translated into tubular MOF-based micromotors by confining SDS within an agarose matrix inside the micromotor cavity. Local surfactant release generates a micelle-rich microenvironment that promotes MOF degradation and cargo release while limiting bulk surfactant exposure and reducing the cytotoxic effects associated with free surfactant under the tested conditions. The resulting platform integrates micelle-mediated MOF disassembly with spatially confined micromotor delivery, providing a strategy for localized and enhanced cargo release from MOF-based dynamic systems.

item.title: Photoinduced Eosin Y Self-Disproportionation Enables Reactivity beyond Direct Excited-State Electron Transfer
item.description:
Abstract
Photoredox catalysis is commonly governed by the redox properties of the initially excited photocatalyst, which can limit the activation of difficult-to-oxidize alkenes. Here, we identify photoinduced self-disproportionation of neutral eosin Y (EH2) as an alternative activation pathway. In fluorinated-alcohol media, specific hydrogen-bonding interactions stabilize a minor population of the visible-light-absorbing EH2_acid tautomer. Following excitation and intersystem crossing, triplet EH2 undergoes intermolecular hydrogen-atom transfer with ground-state EH2 to generate the complementary radicals EH• and EH3•. Time-resolved spectroscopy shows that the alkene substrate does not measurably intercept excited EH2 but instead reacts with the secondary radical EH•, thereby separating photon absorption from substrate activation. Fluorinated alcohols further couple this radical-pair chemistry to productive C–C bond formation, as illustrated by highly selective polyene cyclizations. These findings establish photocatalyst self-disproportionation as a distinct mechanistic pathway that generates secondary reactive species whose reactivity is not accessible via direct excited-state electron transfer.

item.title: Large 77 Se NMR Signal Enhancements in Solutions by Overhauser Dynamic Nuclear Polarization at 9.4 T for Real-Time Reaction Monitoring
item.description:
Abstract
77Se nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) is a key method to probe selenium functional centers in biology and materials science, yet its practical application is severely hindered by its intrinsically low sensitivity due to the low gyromagnetic ratio (19% of 1H) and natural abundance (7.6%). Overhauser effect dynamic nuclear polarization (OE-DNP) has recently emerged as a promising method for generating steady-state signal enhancement in high-field liquid NMR at room temperature. However, its application to 77Se has remained unexplored to date. Here, we present liquid-state OE-DNP as a route for 77Se NMR. At 9.4 T, we report 102 to 103 fold signal enhancements for organoselenium compounds, including the drug candidate ebselen, with polarization buildup within seconds. The large enhancements are the result of efficient electron-to-nuclear polarization transfer with OE-DNP coupling factors of ≳|0.4|, the highest reported so far at high magnetic fields (≥3 T) for NMR-active nuclei. The replenishable signal enhancements allow reaction monitoring by NMR on timescales longer than nuclear T1. As a proof of concept, we monitor a diselenide metathesis reaction over 48 h, capturing species evolution for kinetic studies. This effect can be further expanded to the heavier chalcogen, tellurium, as demonstrated by 123Te OE-DNP with similar efficiency.

item.title: Cross-Linked Halide Networks for Lithium Superionic Conduction
item.description:
Abstract
All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) hold great promise for next-generation energy storage owing to their high safety and energy density, yet their performance critically depends on solid electrolytes (SEs) with high ionic conductivity and structural robustness. Mixed-anion chemistry, exemplified by the Cl/O system, has emerged as an effective approach for designing halide-based superionic conductors, where partial oxygen incorporation distorts the regular halide framework and enhances Li+ mobility. However, we herein show that uncontrolled oxygen incorporation is prone to generate nonbridging oxygens (NBOs), which can hinder Li+ migration via Coulombic interactions. To address this, we develop a polyanion-assisted cross-linking strategy that promotes more bridging-oxygen (BOs) coordination and less formation of NBOs. This yields a highly disordered, frustrated energy landscape conducive to efficient Li+ percolation and rapid ion migration. As an example, PO43– polyanion cross-linked ZrClx halide networks (ZrCl4-xLi3PO4) are developed and exhibit ionic conductivities up to 2.8 × 10–3 S cm–1 at 30 °C, competitive with state-of-the-art rare-metal halides, while maintaining >10–3 S cm–1 after humid exposure (5% RH, 12 h). ASSBs incorporating these electrolytes demonstrate stable cycling not only under elevated temperatures (55 °C) but also under high voltages (4.6 V). These findings identify NBO environments as potential transport inhibitors and establish inorganic cross-linking topochemistry as a structural design principle for robust, high-performance, halide solid electrolytes.

item.title: An Allosteric CLR N-Terminal Swing-Out Mechanism for RAMP-Mediated Adrenomedullin Receptor Selectivity
item.description:
Abstract
Three receptor activity-modifying proteins (RAMP1–3) form heterodimers with the calcitonin (CTR) and calcitonin-like (CLR) G protein-coupled receptors and determine their selectivity for six CGRP family peptide agonists. These ligand–receptor systems are drug targets for migraine headache, diabetes and obesity, and circulatory system disorders. Here, we used molecular dynamics simulations and pharmacological assays of receptor chimeras and point mutants to identify a crucial allosteric component of the mechanism by which RAMP2 and RAMP3 modulate CLR to confer selectivity for two adrenomedullin (AM) peptides. We found that the extracellular domain (ECD) of RAMP2 and RAMP3, but not RAMP1, stabilized a partially unwound “swing-out” conformation of the CLR ECD N-terminal α-helix to accommodate the unique binding mode of the midregion of the AM peptides. The inability of the CTR N-terminus to adopt the swing-out conformation contributed to the distinct peptide selectivity profile of the three CTR-RAMP amylin receptors. By exploiting the CLR swing-out conformation, we engineered AM antagonist peptide variants with enhanced affinity and selectivity for CLR-RAMP2 and -RAMP3. Our results reveal the long-sought mechanism of RAMP-altered CLR ligand selectivity and have significant implications for drug development targeting the CLR- and CTR-RAMP complexes.

item.title: Enantioconvergent N -Alkylation of Indoles with Alcohols Promoted by an Axially Chiral Iridacycle
item.description:
Abstract
Achieving chemo- and enantioselective N-substitution of indoles presents significant challenges for catalytic method development. Herein, we report an enantioconvergent N-substitution of indoles with racemic secondary alcohols enabled by a newly developed axially chiral biaryl-supported iridacycle and chiral phosphoric acid. This borrowing-hydrogen process proceeds through an intriguing sequence involving transfer hydrogenation of indole, enantioselective reductive amination of an indoline intermediate, and subsequent rearomatization. Controlled reaction temperatures also enable selective access to the N-substituted indolines prior to rearomatization. The catalytic process accommodates diverse indoles and unactivated secondary alcohols without additional stoichiometric reagents, providing a direct and atom-economical approach to enantioenriched N-substituted indoles, including analogs of established drug candidates.

item.title: A Unique Conformationally Assisted [2+2] Configuration in Cycloparaphenylenes Enables Efficient Laser Devices
item.description:
Abstract
Two π-conjugated macrocycles, namely the well-known [12]cycloparaphenylene and a newly designed macrocycle combining benzenes and rigid stilbene units, are presented for the first time as light-amplifying gain media in distributed feedback (DFB) laser devices. Both systems show good photonic functionality arising from a four-state photonic cycle comprising a [2+2] state configuration (two delocalized and two conformationally distorted localized states). The mechanism involves the generation of two optically coupled states through excited-state structural distortion induced during internal conversion, which reduces light reabsorption losses and promotes rapid population inversion. Comprehensive steady-state absorption and fluorescence and transient absorption spectroscopy studies are conducted in order to reveal the nature of the low energy lying excited states. Furthermore, amplified spontaneous emission studies of the compounds in polystyrene thin films, followed by the preparation and characterization of optically pumped DFB lasers, were performed. The results reveal new properties of these multifunctional cyclic π-conjugated molecules and unique structure-property relationships.

item.title: Chemical Programming of Stacking Order and Superconductivity Dimensionality in NbSe 2–x Te x Polytypic Heterostructures
item.description:
Abstract
Layered transition-metal dichalcogenides exhibit electronic states highly sensitive to lattice symmetry, yet elucidating the structure–superconductivity relationship has been challenging due to the lack of a continuous structural evolution within a single material system. Here, we establish NbSe2–xTex as a model system, where Te substitution drives a sequential polytypic transition across the full composition range─from the low-Te 2H phase, through mixed 1H/1T heterostructured 4H and 6R polytypes at intermediate substitution, to ideal 1T and distorted 1T′ structures at high Te content. Combining comprehensive characterizations, we map both the structural evolution and the accompanying changes in spectral weight and orbital character near the Fermi level. Electrical transport measurements reveal a striking phase-dependent superconducting dimensionality: the 4H phase (NbSe1.4Te0.6) exhibits enhanced anisotropy and an anomalous boost in the in-plane upper critical field, while the 6R phase (NbSe1.2Te0.8) shows suppressed Tc (∼2.8 K) and three-dimensional-like behavior. The combined electronic-structure and superconducting results connect the stacking sequence to effective interlayer coherence and the local spin–orbit environment. SOC band calculations resolve the distinct symmetry constraints on the 4H and 6R electronic states. These mechanisms fundamentally differ from conventional approaches by leveraging intrinsic, composition-driven polytypism to modify interlayer coupling and band structure. Thus, by establishing a definitive phase diagram that directly correlates polytypism with superconducting dimensionality, our work provides a clear roadmap for the rational design of low-dimensional superconducting devices through stacking-sequence engineering.

item.title: Entropy Engineering Accelerates High-Temperature Oxygen Evolution Reaction Rate via Spin Manipulation
item.description:
Abstract
The high-temperature oxygen evolution reaction (OER) activity is closely correlated to the spin state of transition metals in perovskite anodes. However, the roles of entropy engineering in modulating the spin state and influencing high-temperature OER kinetics remain poorly understood. Herein, we demonstrate that entropy engineering of La0.7Sr0.3FeO3−δ to (SmNdPrLaBaSrCa)FeO3−δ (SNPLBSCF) induces a transition of B-site Fe species from high-spin to low-spin states. This transition enhances the d–p hybridization of Fe–O bonds, lowers the energy barriers for electron transfer and oxygen ion migration, and finally accelerates the high-temperature OER kinetics. Consequently, the SNPLBSCF anode in a solid oxide electrolysis cell (SOEC) achieves a current density of 3.64 A·cm–2 at 800 °C and 1.6 V, outperforming most reported anodes. This work not only provides fundamental insights into the spin state-activity relationships of perovskite oxides but also offers a viable strategy for the rational design of highly efficient SOEC anodes through entropy engineering.

item.title: Nanoscale Flexibility Enables Low-Enthalpy Cooperative Water Sorption
item.description:
Abstract
Passive, sorption-based atmospheric water harvesting technologies (AWHTs) have attracted recent interest as an alternative to energy-intensive condensation-based technologies. Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) offer wide chemical tunability to design sorbents, but in practice, sorbents must retain moisture during humidity fluctuations, and small adsorption enthalpies are necessary for regeneration of the sorbent material. Here, we report that Cu(1,2,3-triazolate)2 nanoparticles with diameters less than 120 nm exhibit structural flexibility at the Cu2+ centers that enables a “breathing”-type cooperative water sorption. This cooperative structural phase change occurs only for nanoparticles that contain Cu2+, and not for the isomorphic magnesium triazolate. The phase change significantly decreases the onset pressures of adsorption and desorption compared to large particles and opens a practically useful hysteresis window in the isotherms, while maintaining small adsorption enthalpies (48 kJ/mol averaged over the isotherm, approaching the 44 kJ/mol latent heat of water at low RH). Mechanistic analysis indicates that adsorption initiates with weak electrostatic and dispersion interactions between water and triazolate rings brought into close proximity only by the distorted Cu2+ centers of the nanoparticles. Together, these results present a distinct water sorption mechanism and design strategy that leverages size- and metal-dependent lattice flexibility in a wide class of porous materials.

item.title: Catalytic Enantiodivergent Neophyl Rearrangement
item.description:
Abstract
The neophyl rearrangement is a long-established radical 1,2-aryl migration, yet catalytic enantioselective control of this process has remained elusive. Here we report a cooperative photoredox and chiral Brønsted acid catalytic system for the enantioselective neophyl rearrangement of tertiary alcohol-derived olefins. The reaction affords 1,5-dicarbonyl compounds bearing azaarene-substituted all-carbon quaternary stereocenters with up to 97% ee. Changing the radical precursor alters the preferred mode of catalyst recognition and reverses the absolute stereochemical outcome with the same catalyst configuration, providing access to opposite product enantiomers. The reaction also accommodates racemic olefin substrates, and experiments with the individual substrate enantiomers show that the chiral catalyst can counter their intrinsic stereochemical preferences. The results reveal how changes in catalyst–substrate recognition can alter stereochemical control during a transient radical rearrangement.

item.title: Halogenated Triazole-Based Metal–Organic Framework Achieves Ultra-Selective CO 2 Capture under Humid Conditions
item.description:
Abstract
Selective CO2 capture from humid, N2-rich flue gas requires adsorbents that combine extreme CO2/N2 discrimination with robustness under realistic conditions. However, only a few MOFs are able to combine ultrahigh selectivity, humidity tolerance, scalable synthesis, and structural durability. Here, we introduce CALF-20-X (X = Cl or Br) halogentriazolate–oxalate Zn-MOFs and a PVDF composite, integrating these attributes into an ultramicroporous framework. The halogenated Zn-MOFs are obtained by means of solvent-minimized liquid-assisted grinding followed by water-incubation route, producing a highly crystalline material. Halogen functionalization polarizes the triazolate C–H donor, thereby promoting directional C–H···O(CO2) contacts and enhancing electrostatic complementarity, as evidenced by an experimental isosteric heat of adsorption of 48 kJ/mol. Furthermore, this halogen substitution significantly restricts the size of the pore window inhibiting N2 uptake, and leads to the formation of perfectly CO2-fitted pockets. These combined features enabled a CO2 excellent adsorption of 2.89 mmol g–1 at 0.15 bar and 298 K, and CO2/N2 selectivity higher than 4074 for CALF-20-Cl, exceeding leading physisorbent benchmarks. The highly selective CO2 capture was confirmed by dynamic breakthrough experiments performed on a CALF-20-Cl@PVDF composite under humid conditions over numerous cycles, thus demonstrating its robust performance under flue-gas-relevant conditions. Competitive CO2/H2O breakthrough experiments, supported by GCMC simulations, demonstrate that CO2 sorption is favored at 21% relative humidity (RH), resulting in a 56% suppression of water uptake, and even remains competitive at RH > 50% and 318 K, a temperature relevant for carbon capture from point sources. These results highlight halogen-driven structural engineering for regenerable and humidity-tolerant next-generation CO2-selective MOF adsorbents with complete retention of the performance metrics.

item.title: Direct-to-Biology Bifunctional Screening Reveals Noncanonical Mechanisms of Targeted Protein Degradation
item.description:
Abstract
Targeted protein degradation (TPD) has emerged as a powerful strategy for modulating protein function through small-molecule-induced proximity between a protein of interest (POI) and typically an E3 ubiquitin ligase to promote its proteasomal degradation. Despite significant progress, most degraders co-opt a narrow set of E3 ubiquitin ligases, motivating mechanistically agnostic strategies for discovering new routes to degradation. Here, we pursued a “degrader-first” approach using direct-to-biology (D2B) synthesis to construct and screen a 114-member library of BRD4-targeting bifunctional molecules to identify chemically tractable ligases that support TPD. Multiple compounds were found to induce Cullin-RING ligase (CRL)-dependent degradation, and two top hits were selected for mechanistic characterization. Unexpectedly, neither operates through canonical heterobifunctional E3 recruitment. Instead, one undergoes oxidative activation to generate a reactive electrophile that promotes degradation through DCAF11- or DCAF16-containing CRL4 complexes in a cell-context-dependent manner. The second acts through a bivalent bromodomain-binding mechanism that likely induces target conformational contraction and potentiates endogenous CRL3–SPOP-mediated ubiquitination. These findings highlight the capacity of D2B discovery approaches to expose noncanonical modalities of TPD while underscoring the importance of rigorous mechanistic deconvolution in interpreting screening-derived degraders.

item.title: Experimental and Computational Identification of Wide-Gap Quaternary Oxychalcogenides BaZn 2 OS 2 and SrZn 2 OSe 2
item.description:
Abstract
Oxychalcogenides have attracted attention as candidates for wide-gap p-type semiconductors in view of the energetically high and spatially spread characteristics of their valence electronic states. An appropriate choice of constituent cations would also enable n-type doping. However, reports on p-type doping have been mostly limited to Cu-based systems, which exhibit a strong p-type tendency due to hole generation and electron compensation by native Cu-vacancy acceptors. Oxychalcogenides with a practical level of n-type conductivity are yet to be developed. In this study, we focus on oxychalcogenides in the Ae–Zn–O–Ch (Ae = Ca, Sr, Ba; Ch = S, Se) quaternary system to explore new wide-gap semiconductors. Two as-yet-unreported compounds with wide band gaps, namely BaZn2OS2 and SrZn2OSe2, have been synthesized, along with four previously reported oxychalcogenides. First-principles calculations indicate that both BaZn2OS2 and SrZn2OSe2 feature direct-type band structures with low electron and hole effective masses, comparable to related compounds. Carrier compensation by native defects, however, is likely to make BaZn2OS2 insulating, whereas it can be well suppressed in SrZn2OSe2 by controlling the growth conditions. Systematic calculations of extrinsic dopants predict that bipolar doping of SrZn2OSe2 is feasible. Our results reveal the potential of non-Cu-based oxychalcogenides as a platform for the development of wide-gap, bipolar-dopable semiconductors, thereby stimulating exploration of related compounds.

item.title: NMR Reveals Coupled Ligand and Protein Conformational Equilibria That Modulate the Affinity of MDM2-Inhibitory Peptoids
item.description:
Abstract
Peptoids, atypical peptides with N-substitutions, are a promising drug modality for targeting protein–protein interactions. The binding affinity of an MDM2-inhibitory peptoid decreases by more than 100-fold upon removal of the backbone-restricting methyl groups attached to the α-carbons, although this modification alters the population of the all-trans amide-bond isomer by only 1.6-fold. This discrepancy raises the possibility that backbone flexibility affects not only ligand preorganization but also the conformational ensemble of the target protein. Here, we used NMR to examine the binding mode of the MDM2-peptoid complexes. ZZ-exchange experiments demonstrated that peptoid isomers containing cis amide bonds bind less favorably to MDM2 than the all-trans amide bond isomer. In addition, observation of the I19 δ1-methyl resonance of MDM2 in complex with the peptoids revealed that MDM2 exists in equilibrium between an open state, corresponding to the crystal structure of the MDM2-peptoid complex, and a semiclosed state, which retains partial interactions between the N-terminal region of MDM2 and the ligand-binding cleft. Increased population of the semiclosed state correlated with reduced binding affinities of the peptoids. We propose that cis-trans isomerization of the peptoid amide bonds and the conformational equilibrium of MDM2 within the peptoid complex synergistically contribute to the more than 100-fold decrease in binding affinity. These results identify coupled ligand and protein conformational equilibria as determinants of binding affinity and suggest conformational-plasticity control as a potential design principle for oligomeric ligands targeting protein–protein interactions.

item.title: Radical Ring-Opening Polymerization of endo -Cyclic Monomers for Regioregularity Control in Vinyl Polymers
item.description:
Abstract
Radical polymerization of vinyl monomers is inherently governed by propagation pathways that favor head-to-tail connectivity, limiting access to alternative backbone regioregularities. To address this challenge, we report the radical ring-opening polymerization (rROP) of endo-cyclic monomers, a class of monomers that has been largely unexplored in radical processes. Whereas many established rROP systems have been designed to introduce functional or cleavable units into polymer backbones, the present endo-cyclic monomers undergo selective rROP to generate carbon–carbon-backboned vinyl polymers enriched with nonhead-to-tail linkages. Copolymerization with conventional vinyl monomers was also achieved, providing access to copolymers with tunable backbone microstructures. In particular, using vinyl ketones and their corresponding endo-cyclic cyclodimers as structurally matched pairs, we accessed poly(vinyl ketone)s with systematically varied head-to-tail linkage contents. This control over backbone regioregularity translated into tunable macroscopic properties, including glass transition temperature and photodegradation kinetics, establishing regioregularity as a structural handle for controlling material properties. The strategy was also compatible with controlled radical polymerization, enabling the synthesis of well-defined block copolymers. Micelles assembled from these block copolymers further exhibited regioregularity-dependent sizes and photoresponsive behavior. These findings establish endo-cyclic rROP as a previously unrecognized strategy for controlling backbone regioregularity and properties in vinyl polymers.

item.title: G:C:G:C-Flanked i-Motifs Are Thermodynamically Favored and Their Sequences Highly Enriched in the Human Genome
item.description:
Abstract
i-Motifs are biologically relevant noncanonical DNA structures whose stability is strongly influenced by capping interactions. Among these, minor groove tetrads (MGTs) are among the most powerful stabilizing elements identified to date, yet the molecular factors governing their effects and their potential biological significance remain poorly understood. Here, we present a systematic experimental and computational analysis of 16 MGT-stabilized i-motifs (MGTiMs), encompassing all combinations of terminal tetrad composition and orientation within a common sequence scaffold. NMR spectroscopy confirms that all sequences adopt closely related architectures, enabling direct comparison of the effects of tetrad identity and orientation on stability. Thermal denaturation experiments reveal that the stability hierarchy, previously observed in selected structures (G:C:G:C ≳ G:C:G:T ≫ G:T:G:T), is broadly maintained across the series, although substantial positional effects are observed. Molecular dynamics simulations and energy decomposition analyses suggest that differences in electrostatic interactions and local conformational flexibility contribute to these trends. Notably, genome-wide analysis of the human genome reveals a strong enrichment of sequences capable of forming the most stabilizing tetrads, with motifs containing two G:C:G:C tetrads reaching a 45-fold enrichment relative to random expectation. Interestingly, this most abundant genomic motif is also the only one that undergoes pronounced pH-driven conformational transitions, highlighting the unique structural plasticity of these architectures. Together, these findings reveal how tetrad composition and positional context govern MGTiM stability and identify NN-type motifs as a particularly enriched class of structurally distinctive genomic sequences.

item.title: Elusive *CH–*CHO Coupling Pathway for High-Performance CO 2 Electroreduction to n-Propanol
item.description:
Abstract
The electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to high-value n-propanol represents a promising yet challenging route toward sustainable carbon utilization. However, its practical implementation is severely hindered by low selectivity and activity, primarily originating from the high energy barrier involved in the rate-limiting *C2–*C1 coupling step. Herein, we have successfully constructed an elusive *CH–*CHO coupling pathway on a stable Janus Cu2+/Cu0 catalyst, enabling low-barrier *C2 intermediate formation and highly selective n-propanol production. Leveraging the strong electron-accepting capacity of Cu2+ sites, key *CHO intermediates are strongly adsorbed and driven toward deep reduction to *CH species, effectively overcoming the critical five-electron transfer bottleneck for *CH generation. Meanwhile, adjacent Cu0 sites provide moderate and balanced adsorption of *CHO intermediates, allowing their asymmetric coupling with the Cu2+-stabilized *CH via a markedly low energy barrier, synergistically steering the reaction along the favorable *CH–*CHO pathway. In situ fiber-optic guided ATR-FTIR spectroscopy provides evidence for the coexistence of *CHO and *CHx-related intermediates, while DFT calculations further support the proposed *CH–*CHO coupling pathway. Accordingly, the Janus Cu2+/Cu0 catalyst achieves a high n-propanol Faradaic efficiency of 18.1% at a partial current density of 72.4 mA cm–2, alongside remarkable stability. This work establishes the *CH–*CHO pathway as a powerful strategy for kinetically favorable C–C coupling, opening a new mechanistic avenue for efficient conversion of CO2 to multicarbon via electrosynthesis.

item.title: Hypoxia-Driven, Self-Accelerating Immolative Photosensitizer Enabling Effective and Safe Photodynamic Therapy
item.description:
Abstract
Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is an emerging cancer treatment modality, but its clinical translation is hindered by the persistent post-PDT phototoxicity of existing photosensitizers. To address this challenge, we herein report a hypoxia-driven, self-accelerating immolative photosensitizer in which PDT itself drives posttherapy detoxification. This is demonstrated with AIE photosensitizers with an N-oxidation-mediated photoinduced electron transfer (PET) feature, which creates a charge-separation state with pronounced electron–nuclear hyperfine coupling feature, enabling efficient intersystem crossing. This N-oxidation thus converts the highly emissive fluorophore TBP into the robust type I photosensitizer TBPO. Critically, the N-O bond could be selectively cleaved by cytochrome P450 reductases under hypoxia, immolating TBPO back to TBP. Unlike previously reported ROS-driven immolative photosensitizers, this hypoxia-mediated immolation does not consume therapeutic ROS and is accelerated by PDT-aggravated hypoxia. Consequently, TBPO exhibits a self-propelled detoxification mechanism, ensuring an initial high PDT efficacy while minimizing residual phototoxicity after therapy. Moreover, this transition process is self-reported by the fluorescence light-up. This molecular design achieves both potent hypoxia-resistant PDT and fail-safe posttreatment safety, addressing two long-standing barriers to clinical PDT. This paradigm shift offers a general design principle for therapy-fueled self-detoxifying photosensitizers toward outpatient PDT without lifestyle restrictions.

item.title: Phosphate-Mediated Proton Shuttling Governs Nitrate Electroreduction Selectivity on Copper
item.description:
Abstract
The electrochemical reduction of nitrate (NO3RR) can be carried out at high reaction rates, yet selectivity to desired ammonia/ammonium remains challenging on catalysts like copper due to a soluble nitrite intermediate. We here find the local microenvironment of NO3RR can influence typical catalyst metrics of rate and selectivity to extents on par with those typically attributed to differences in catalyst formulation. Considering a phosphate-buffered pH 7 medium, we find the high NO3RR rates on Cu exceed the buffering capacity, leading to a surface pH ∼ 13. Accounting for the local proton activity to measure reaction rates at fixed overpotential demonstrates rates approximately an order of magnitude greater compared to a bulk pH 13 electrolyte. In the absence of phosphate, nitrite is kinetically more difficult to reduce on Cu than is nitrate. Inclusion of phosphate─regardless of the bulk pH─leads to the onset of nitrite reduction at comparable potentials to nitrate reduction, and ∼2× higher electron selectivity to ammonia/ammonium compared to without phosphate. Grand canonical density functional theory calculations and microkinetic modeling demonstrate that adsorbed phosphate thermodynamically favors proton abstraction from water under reaction conditions, whereas nitrate and nitrite are incapable of doing so. This effectively leads to a surface-mediated pKa of phosphate species that is different than in solution, which changes the local population of hydrogenated phosphates that can participate in proton-transfer events. This adsorbed phosphate─observed by operando surface-enhanced infrared spectroscopy─stabilizes the nitrite intermediate and promotes proton shuttling from water to nitrite, increasing selectivity to ammonia. The presence of a pH gradient further promotes proton shuttling from the bulk electrolyte to exacerbate these trends. Overall, these findings highlight that surface-mediated processes can strongly impact the effective pKa of adsorbed ions relative to those in solution, and can provide additional routes for leveraging the local environment in catalyst design.

item.title: Turnovers Drive Supported Metal Nanoparticle Catalyst Surface Reconstruction to Kinetically Trapped Metastable Structures
item.description:
Abstract
Supported metal catalysts often operate with high adsorbate coverages that can alter nanoparticle structures as compared to the clean catalyst. Such restructuring is typically described within an equilibrium picture that assumes that nanoparticle structures and adsorbate coverages adopt their thermodynamically preferred state. Here, we challenge this assumption and propose that under conditions of high adsorbate coverage and fast turnovers of surface species, supported metal nanoparticle structures and adsorbate coverages can become kinetically trapped in metastable states. We studied CO adsorption–desorption quasi-equilibrium on Pt/γ-Al2O3 using in situ IR spectroscopy and chemisorption as a function of temperature (300–650 K), CO pressure (10–2–10–4 bar), and visible photon flux (0–2 W cm–2 440 nm photons). The adsorbed CO IR band area increases with temperature and photon flux, contrary to equilibrium predictions of decreasing coverage. Estimates of apparent Pt dispersion and CO desorption rates, along with the reversibility of IR spectral changes, support the hypothesis that when CO turnovers are faster than Pt atomic rearrangements to their equilibrium state, the catalyst is driven into metastable states. We estimate atomic rearrangements time scales of 10–1–10–3 s on CO-covered Pt nanoparticles at ∼500–600 K. Grand-canonical sampling calculations show that equilibrium Pt–CO structures cannot reproduce the experimental IR trends, implying the presence of off-equilibrium coverages, structures, or both. By matching the experimental trend, theory identifies a plausible flat, nonequilibrium free-energy region that can facilitate kinetic trapping of metastable catalyst states. These results highlight the need for theoretical and experimental approaches targeting nonequilibrium structures to establish structure–function relationships in heterogeneous catalysis.

item.title: Structural Evolution Accompanies Selectivity Changes during the Electrocatalytic Reduction of CO 2 on a Vicinal Cu(310) Pre-Catalyst
item.description:
Abstract
The electrocatalytic reduction reaction of CO2 (CO2RR) on copper remains a key strategy for converting greenhouse gases into valuable chemicals, but its large-scale implementation still requires substantial advances in our fundamental understanding of the selectivity-determining properties. Historically, stepped Cu surfaces were thought to have great potential for selective hydrocarbon production during CO2RR. However, it has recently become clear that this distinct facet dependence does not hold for atomically flat Cu(100) and (111) surfaces with large terraces, which primarily yield hydrogen. The present study addresses how the crystallographic orientation and surface history influence CO2RR performance over Cu(310), a vicinal surface with an intrinsically higher density of step-edge defects. Our results show striking analogies to the nonvicinal surfaces, namely, an initially large H2 selectivity but also the formation during operation of mesoscopic imperfections that play a crucial role in the surface activation and catalytic selectivity toward hydrocarbons. More importantly, we report the deactivation mechanism of our vicinal surface upon extended CO2RR operation, which switches from hydrocarbon formation back to hydrogen. Additionally, we demonstrate how the desired hydrocarbon-product selectivity can be regenerated via in situ electrochemical oxidative treatments. Finally, substantial differences in the deactivation kinetics toward H2 evolution vs CO2RR, depending on the oxidative treatment employed, are unveiled. These findings establish a clear link between surface mesoscale morphology, oxidation dynamics, and catalytic function, highlighting the need for controlled surface/chemical state engineering in CO2RR catalysts. These insights offer practical guidance for designing more stable and efficient copper-based systems for CO2 conversion.

item.title: Supramolecular Hexaphyrin Cage: Cooperative Guest Binding and Reversible Aromaticity Switching by Proton-Coupled Electron Transfer
item.description:
Abstract
Coordination-driven self-assembly of a rigidified, antiaromatic β,β’-linked hexaphyrin ligand (1) bearing three meso-pyridyl donors with a trans-platinum(II) diacceptor corner (2) affords a discrete trigonal-prismatic metal–organic cage, CHP, in which two cofacial hexaphyrin decks are held rigidly apart by three Pt(II)-based coordination bridges. Multinuclear NMR spectroscopy, high-resolution ESI-MS, and DOSY establish the assembly as a single, highly symmetric [2 + 3] species, with a solution-state hydrodynamic radius consistent with the DFT-optimized geometry. Electrochemical and spectroelectrochemical studies reveal that CHP undergoes a reversible proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) process, interconverting between a 24π-antiaromatic and a 26π-aromatic Hückel state upon combined treatment with a proton source and a mild chemical or electrochemical reductant, demonstrating that the switching behavior of the parent hexaphyrin is preserved within the confined 3D architecture. Furthermore, the electron-poor internal cavity of CHP encapsulates two planar zinc(II) porphyrazine guests in a discrete 1:2 host–guest complex with positive cooperativity, as quantified by UV–vis titration. This work establishes a strategy for embedding the electronic responsiveness of expanded porphyrinoids within discrete, functional supramolecular hosts.

item.title: Charge-Transfer Dynamics in Ternary Organic Photovoltaic Materials Containing Nonfullerene Acceptors: Role of Reaction Temperature
item.description:
Abstract
Ternary organic photovoltaic devices incorporating A-D-A type nonfullerene acceptors offer promising enhancements in power conversion efficiency. However, fabrication conditions can introduce impurities that disrupt molecular packing and the charge-transfer (CT) dynamics, thereby reducing performance and stability.
